title: The woman who killed Marat, and why the court wouldn't believe she acted alone
dek: Corday had her declaration written before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone — yet the revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy." They could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.
why: High information density: it strings the institutional origins of the Terror, paper-money inflation and the Vendée war into a single causal chain, and the back half on the assassination details is especially valuable.
who: Listeners interested in the French Revolution, the origins of the Terror, and the mechanics of political violence; readers who want to understand how populist language and revolutionary institutions get improvised.
skip: The last two minutes are a trailer for another podcast, with no historical content — skip straight past it.

points.h: The assassination declaration was written before the act
points.body: When Corday was arrested she was carrying a declaration titled "To the Friends of Law and Peace in France." In it she named Marat "the most vile scoundrel," said he "has been condemned by the universe, and is therefore outside the law," and called on the French to "rise up. Strike. Strike." This text was not a post-hoc defence — it was written before the act. What she wanted was not escape, but to turn her own death into a rallying point.

points.h: Marat was the first modern populist
points.body: Keith Michael Baker's new biography positions Marat as the first modern populist. His recipe included: constantly invoking the capital-P "People," and claiming the people are at every moment in danger of being betrayed by appeasers and traitors; an obsession with conspiracy theory, openly stating that his goal was to keep his readers "perpetually on their guard," lest they be dragged into the abyss by royalists, priests and their ilk. The show points out that this "wake up, sheep" language is used by both left and right today.

points.h: Paper-money inflation pushed the poor into the streets
points.body: In early 1793 France had years of poor harvests, the national grain market collapsed, and the government had no money to fight the war, so it printed paper money — the assignat — with about four billion in circulation. This triggered severe inflation, bread and sugar prices soared, there were protests in the market almost daily, and women's marches appeared in the streets of Paris. The show stresses: these were exactly the same conditions that had set off the Revolution and the storming of the Bastille, and the poor would think, "the Revolution happened, yet life hasn't improved — so someone must be scheming."

points.h: The commander-in-chief's defection confirmed the conspiracy theories
points.body: On 8 March 1793 the Austrians counter-attacked, crushing Dumouriez at Neerwinden, and he was forced to withdraw from Belgium and Holland. He wanted to imitate Sulla and march on Paris as a military dictator, and asked his troops, "Shall we march on Paris?" They answered no. On 5 April he rode over to the Austrian lines, taking a number of senior officers with him, including the future King of France, Louis Philippe. One volunteer wrote to his mother: "Who can we trust now?"

points.h: The Terror machine was improvised, not designed
points.body: The show stresses that the key institutions of the Terror had no blueprint and no plan — they were built as they went, and only in hindsight assembled into a machine, and many of those who helped build it were eventually swallowed by it. On 10 March the Revolutionary Tribunal was established to try political crimes, with death sentences to be carried out within 24 hours and no right of appeal, housed in the Palais de Justice in Paris, with the existing Conciergerie cells in its basement. Danton said: "Let us be terrible, so that the people need not be."

points.h: The Girondins used a new rule to strike at Marat, and it backfired
points.body: The Girondins had just abolished parliamentary immunity, and while large numbers of deputies were away in the provinces, they indicted Marat on 14 April, accusing him of inciting insurrection. Marat went into hiding for three days, then found that public opinion in the streets of Paris was on his side, and simply turned himself in for trial. On 24 April the court convened in the Palais de Justice; the prosecutor, Fuquietanville, was a Montagnard supporter and let Marat deliver a long defence. The ten-man jury acquitted him within a few hours, and Marat was carried back to the National Convention by some 800 people, crowned with roses, with cries of "vive la république, vive Marat." For the Girondins it was a total humiliation.

points.h: Corday buys a knife: a 15cm black-handled kitchen knife
points.body: At around eight in the morning on 13 July, Charlotte Corday left her hotel, walked to the arcades of the Palais-Royal, bought a newspaper (which said the Convention would likely sentence the imprisoned Girondin deputies to death), and bought a black Paris hat with a green ribbon, replacing the white Norman-style hat that marked her out. She went into a cutlery shop called Le Coutelier Badin and bought a kitchen knife with a black handle and a blade about 15 centimetres long. Between 11:30 and noon she took a carriage to Marat's home on the rue des Cordeliers, but she had no appointment and was turned away by Marat's sister-in-law.

points.h: The court wouldn't believe a woman could act alone
points.body: Corday was arrested on the spot, and one of her interrogators was Jean-Baptiste Drouet, the postmaster who had recognised Louis XVI's flight at Varennes. From the start she said she had acted alone. But the revolutionary tribunal repeatedly interrogated her about the "chain of conspiracy," convinced she must be part of a Girondin plot. The interrogator Montané said: that's impossible, because you say Marat is the source of all France's ills, yet Marat is precisely the man who never stopped exposing traitors and conspirators, so someone must have lied to you. Corday replied: you're mad — only in Paris do people see Marat; in the other provinces he is taken for a monster. The court could not imagine that provincials would think Marat a bad man.
